title: Introduction to Operating Systems & System Calls
raw_notes: An operating system acts as an intermediary between the user of a computer and the computer hardware. The primary goals of an OS are convenience, efficiency, and safety. Dual-mode operation is implemented using a hardware mode bit: User Mode (bit 1) and Kernel/Supervisor Mode (bit 0). Privileged instructions can only execute in kernel mode. When a user application requires hardware services such as reading a file or sending a network packet, it invokes a system call. A system call triggers a software interrupt or trap. The CPU hardware saves process state, changes the mode bit from 1 to 0, and jumps to a predefined interrupt vector in the kernel. Once the kernel verifies the parameters and completes the service routine, it executes a return-from-trap instruction, restoring user registers and resetting the mode bit to 1. Architectures range from monolithic kernels (Linux) where all services run in a single address space, to microkernels (Minix, Mach) which keep only IPC, low-level memory, and scheduling in kernel mode.

title: Process Management & Process Control Block (PCB)
raw_notes: A process is fundamentally an active program in execution. Unlike passive code sitting on secondary storage, a process contains program text, data section with global variables, heap for dynamic memory, and a stack containing function frames and local variables. The operating system represents each process using a Process Control Block (PCB). The PCB contains critical records: PID, process state, program counter, CPU registers, memory limits, list of open file descriptors, and scheduling priority. Processes transition through five canonical states: New, Ready, Running, Waiting (Blocked for I/O), and Terminated. A context switch occurs when the CPU scheduler switches execution from one running process to another. The OS saves the current process context into its PCB and restores the state of the scheduled process from its PCB. Context switching is pure overhead because the system does no useful computational work while switching. Heavy context switching also flushes CPU translation lookaside buffers and L1/L2 caches.

title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SJF, RR)
raw_notes: CPU scheduling is the basis of multiprogrammed operating systems. By switching the CPU among processes, the OS maximizes CPU utilization. Metrics evaluated in university exams include: Turnaround Time (Completion Time minus Arrival Time), Waiting Time (Turnaround Time minus Burst Time), and Response Time. First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) is non-preemptive and simple, but suffers from the Convoy Effect where short processes wait behind a massive CPU-bound process. Shortest Job First (SJF) is mathematically optimal for minimizing average waiting time, but future CPU bursts cannot be known in advance and must be estimated via exponential smoothing. Preemptive SJF is known as Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). Priority Scheduling allocates CPU to the highest priority process; its primary pitfall is starvation, resolved by Aging where priority increments over time. Round Robin (RR) gives each process a fixed time slice or quantum. If the quantum is too large, RR degenerates into FCFS; if the quantum is too small, context switch overhead dominates the system throughput.

title: Process Synchronization & Semaphores
raw_notes: Concurrent processes sharing memory can enter a race condition where the final outcome depends on the exact execution interleaving. The Critical Section Problem requires any solution to satisfy three mandatory properties: Mutual Exclusion (only one process in critical section), Progress (selection of entering process cannot be postponed indefinitely by outside processes), and Bounded Waiting (a limit exists on how many times other processes enter before a waiting process is granted access). Software solutions include Peterson's Algorithm for two processes. Hardware mechanisms provide atomic instructions such as TestAndSet and CompareAndSwap. Edsger Dijkstra introduced the Semaphore, an integer variable accessed exclusively through atomic operations wait() (P) and signal() (V). Counting semaphores control access to a finite pool of resources, while binary semaphores act as mutual exclusion locks (mutex). Classic synchronization challenges include the Bounded-Buffer (Producer-Consumer), Readers-Writers problem, and the Dining Philosophers dilemma.

title: Deadlock Detection, Prevention & Banker's Algorithm
raw_notes: A deadlock is a condition where a set of processes are permanently blocked because each process holds resources and waits for resources acquired by another process in the same set. Four Coffman conditions must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to arise: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. Deadlock prevention invalidates at least one condition (e.g., ordering all resources numerically to break circular wait). Deadlock avoidance dynamically examines resource allocation state to ensure Circular Wait never occurs. Edsger Dijkstra's Banker's Algorithm tests for safety before granting any resource request. The system maintains Available vector, Max matrix, Allocation matrix, and computes the Need matrix (Need = Max - Allocation). A state is defined as safe if there exists at least one safe execution sequence P1, P2, ..., Pn such that for each process Pi, its maximum remaining need can be satisfied by Available plus the resources already held by preceding processes.

title: Memory Management & Paging
raw_notes: Memory management bridges physical RAM and the CPU's memory requests. Contiguous allocation schemes lead to external fragmentation where total free memory exceeds a process request, but storage is fragmented into non-contiguous pieces. Non-contiguous Paging solves external fragmentation. Physical memory is divided into fixed-size blocks called Frames, and logical address space is divided into same-sized blocks called Pages. The Memory Management Unit (MMU) uses a Page Table to translate a logical address (Page Number p, Offset d) into a physical address (Frame Number f, Offset d). Paging eliminates external fragmentation but exhibits internal fragmentation in the final page of a process. Accessing the page table in memory doubles memory access time. To alleviate this, CPUs implement a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), a fast associative hardware cache. Effective Memory Access Time (EMAT) is computed as: EMAT = Hit_Rate * (TLB_access + RAM_access) + (1 - Hit_Rate) * (TLB_access + 2 * RAM_access).

title: Virtual Memory & Page Replacement (LRU, FIFO, OPT)
raw_notes: Virtual memory allows processes to execute without being completely loaded into physical memory. This allows programs to exceed physical RAM limits and increases degree of multiprogramming. Demand paging loads pages only when referenced. If a process attempts to access a page marked invalid in the page table, a Page Fault exception traps to the OS kernel. The OS locates the page on backing store disk, finds a free frame, reads the page from disk, updates the page table, and restarts the trapped instruction. When no free frame exists, a Page Replacement Algorithm selects a victim frame. FIFO (First-In, First-Out) replaces the oldest page; FIFO exhibits Belady's Anomaly where allocating more physical frames counter-intuitively causes more page faults. Optimal Page Replacement (OPT) replaces the page that will not be used for the longest future duration; OPT serves as an unachievable theoretical benchmark. Least Recently Used (LRU) replaces the page unused for the longest past period and belongs to the class of stack algorithms immune to Belady's Anomaly. Thrashing occurs when a computer spends more time paging in and out than executing instructions.

title: File Systems & Directory Structures
raw_notes: The file system provides persistent, structured, and user-friendly storage on physical secondary storage. Files are abstract data collections with attributes including name, type, size, protection permissions, and timestamps. Directory organizations have evolved from single-level and two-level directories to tree-structured and acyclic-graph directories allowing file sharing via links (hard links pointing directly to the inode vs symbolic/soft links pointing to paths). Disk block allocation strategies include: Contiguous Allocation (fast sequential access but severe external fragmentation and fixed file growth limits), Linked Allocation (no external fragmentation, files grow dynamically, but slow random seek and pointer reliability risk), and Indexed Allocation where an index block contains pointers to data blocks. The Unix file system utilizes an Inode structure with direct block pointers, single indirect pointers, double indirect pointers, and triple indirect pointers to support massive file sizes efficiently.

title: Disk Scheduling Algorithms (SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK)
raw_notes: In mechanical hard disk drives, the access time is dominated by Seek Time (moving the disk read/write head to the desired cylinder) and Rotational Latency (waiting for the sector to rotate beneath the head). Disk scheduling algorithms order pending I/O requests to minimize total head movement. First-Come First-Served (FCFS) is fair but incurs wild arm oscillations. Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF) selects the pending request closest to current head position; while average seek time drops, outer cylinders risk starvation. The SCAN algorithm (Elevator) starts at one end of the disk and moves toward the other end, servicing requests along the way, before reversing at the disk boundary. Circular SCAN (C-SCAN) moves in one direction only; when it reaches the boundary, it jumps immediately back to cylinder zero without servicing requests on the return trip, providing uniform waiting times. LOOK and C-LOOK optimize SCAN and C-SCAN by reversing or returning as soon as the final pending request in that direction has been satisfied, avoiding useless sweeps to disk boundaries.

title: OS Protection, Security & Access Matrix
raw_notes: Protection is an internal mechanism that controls process and user access to defined system resources. Security addresses broader defenses against external threats, malicious penetration, and unauthorized data destruction. The foundational guideline is the Principle of Least Privilege: programs, users, and systems should operate using only the minimal set of privileges necessary to perform their legitimate task. Access rights are formally represented via an Access Matrix where rows designate Protection Domains and columns designate Objects (files, memory segments, devices). Cells specify the access operations permitted (read, write, execute, own). Because access matrices are sparse in practical systems, they are decomposed into: Access Control Lists (ACLs) associated with each Object listing valid domains and permissions, or Capability Lists associated with each Domain listing unforgeable tokens granting specific rights to objects.
